output.title: What churn signals hide before the customer leaves
output.body:
Most churn does not arrive as a dramatic cancellation. It usually shows up in quieter signals: fewer orders, longer gaps between purchases, repeated support questions, or a customer who stops using one part of the service and keeps paying out of habit. The job is not to chase every wobble. It is to separate active signals from passive erosion.

Active signals are the obvious ones: a cancellation notice, a payment problem, a sharp complaint. Those need a human decision now. Passive signals are slower and easier to miss. In a small online shop, an illustrative example is a customer who bought every week and then goes three weeks with no order. That is not proof of churn, but it is a warning worth checking.

The bounded workflow decision is simple: look at the data you already have in a spreadsheet, CRM, support inbox, or payment records, and decide which signals should be flagged for manual review. If the pattern is already in the system, a small workflow can surface it. It should not decide the response on its own. Human approval stays in charge.

A practical next step: pull the last 12 months of order history, support tickets, login activity, and payment records, then pick two or three customers who left or went quiet. Write down the first signal you could have seen at the time. That manual audit will show whether the issue is a real workflow gap or just a feeling wearing a trench coat.
